After several years of contemplation by his predecessors, the president of Cuba has given the green light to gradually eliminate the convertible peso by combining it with the Cuban peso.

When the Soviet Union collapsed, Cuba’s economy went with it. To help deal with the economic downfall of the Special Period in the mid-1990s, the government created a new currency that was pegged to the dollar – the convertible peso – in addition to the normal Cuban peso. Tourists and international trade regularly used the convertible peso due to its higher purchasing power and similarity to the dollar, while Cuban citizens were forced to use the Cuban peso (for comparison, the Cuban peso is roughly equivalent to four cents). Having two currencies allowed the government to isolate both its socialist economy and its citizens from outside pressures.

The process will likely take several years to complete (estimated to be mostly finished some time in 2026), and the first step is allowing government-run stores that used to exclusively use the convertible peso to also accept the Cuban peso. The exchange rate between the currencies is expected to remain the same throughout the process, which means goods won’t become easier to acquire for Cuban citizens. However, despite that fact, the move is seen as an effort to reduce inequality and favoritism of Cubans who work in the tourism industry.
